Cannabis and Anxiety: What the Research Actually Says

By HowToEdibles Editorial Team March 5, 2026 7 min read

Explore what scientific research says about cannabis and anxiety. Learn how THC and CBD affect anxiety differently, optimal dosing strategies, and harm reduction tips.

Home / Articles / Cannabis and Anxiety: What the Research Actually Says

Short answer

Cannabis can both ease and trigger anxiety, depending on the dose. In a controlled 2017 study, 7.5 mg of oral THC reduced distress during a stress test while 12.5 mg increased negative mood, and single doses of CBD (300 mg in healthy volunteers, 600 mg in people with social anxiety disorder) reduced public-speaking anxiety in small trials. A 2019 meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry, however, found little evidence that cannabinoids treat anxiety disorders, and neither THC nor CBD is FDA-approved for anxiety.

Not medical advice

This article is general education, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using cannabis for anxiety, especially if you take other medications (CBD can interact with many of them), are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a history of mental illness or substance use. If your anxiety is severe or you are in crisis, call or text 988 in the U.S.

Anxiety is one of the most commonly cited reasons people turn to cannabis. Surveys consistently show that stress and anxiety relief rank among the top motivations for both medical and recreational use. Yet cannabis has a complicated relationship with anxiety — it can be both the remedy and the trigger. Understanding this paradox requires looking beyond anecdotes and into the growing body of scientific research on cannabinoids and the anxious brain.

The biphasic effect of cannabis on anxiety

The single most important concept for understanding cannabis and anxiety is the biphasic effect — the phenomenon where a substance produces opposite effects at low versus high doses. With cannabis, this means that a small amount of THC may calm your nerves, while a large amount of the same compound can send your heart racing and your thoughts spiraling.

This is not just anecdotal. A 2017 study of 42 healthy volunteers from the University of Illinois at Chicago and the University of Chicago, published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence, confirmed the biphasic pattern in a controlled laboratory setting. Participants who received a low oral dose of THC (7.5 mg) reported less distress after a stressful mock job interview and math task, while those who received a higher dose (12.5 mg) reported more negative mood overall, before and during the task. The difference between relaxation and distress was just five milligrams.

The biphasic effect occurs because THC activates CB1 receptors in the endocannabinoid system. At low concentrations, this activation enhances the natural calming signals that your brain uses to regulate fear and stress responses. At high concentrations, the same receptors become overstimulated, disrupting the delicate balance and producing anxiety, paranoia, and in some cases full-blown panic attacks.

CBD as an anxiolytic

Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as one of the most promising natural compounds for anxiety relief, and its mechanism is fundamentally different from THC. CBD does not directly activate CB1 receptors, which means it does not produce intoxication and does not carry the same risk of triggering paranoia or panic.

Instead, CBD appears to work through multiple pathways. In laboratory studies it activates serotonin 5-HT1A receptors — the same target as buspirone, a prescription anti-anxiety medication. It also modulates the endocannabinoid system indirectly by inhibiting the enzyme FAAH, which breaks down anandamide, your body's natural "bliss molecule." Higher levels of anandamide are associated with reduced anxiety and improved mood.

A pivotal 2019 study published in The Permanente Journal followed 72 adults with anxiety and sleep concerns who were given CBD. Within the first month, anxiety scores decreased in 79.2% of patients and remained lower throughout the study, although the study was open-label with no control group, so the results need confirmation in randomized trials. Neuroimaging research has also shown that CBD reduces activity in the amygdala and anterior cingulate cortex — brain regions that become hyperactive during anxiety states.

CBD is not intoxicating, which makes it a more forgiving option than THC for people who are new to cannabis or sensitive to anxiety. Its dose-response, however, is not simply "more is better." In a 2019 study of 57 healthy men given a simulated public-speaking test, 300 mg of CBD reduced anxiety, while 150 mg and 600 mg did not differ from placebo, an inverted U-shaped curve. CBD also has side effects: the FDA warns that it can cause drowsiness and liver injury and can change how other medications work.

THC dose and the anxiety relationship

THC is not inherently anxiogenic — it is dose-dependent. Understanding this relationship is critical for anyone using cannabis who is prone to anxiety. The general guidelines from research suggest the following pattern:

Microdose range (1–2.5 mg THC): Most users experience subtle relaxation and mood elevation with minimal cognitive impairment. This range is generally considered the safest starting point for anxiety-prone individuals.

Low dose range (2.5–5 mg THC): Noticeable calming effects, mild euphoria, and reduced stress for many people. This is the usual starting range recommended for new edible users. (The 2017 Chicago study above found stress relief at 7.5 mg; it did not test doses this low.)

Moderate dose range (5–15 mg THC): Effects become more variable and individual. Some users still find relief, but the risk of anxiety increases significantly, particularly for people with low tolerance, those new to cannabis, or individuals with a personal or family history of anxiety disorders.

High dose range (15+ mg THC): The probability of anxiety, paranoia, and panic increases substantially. Even experienced users can find themselves overwhelmed at this level, particularly with edibles, where the onset is delayed and the effects are more intense due to the liver converting THC into the more potent metabolite 11-hydroxy-THC.

What the studies show

The body of research on cannabis and anxiety has grown significantly over the past decade, but the strongest evidence is still limited. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry pooled 83 studies of cannabinoids for mental health conditions, 31 of them on anxiety. It found only very low-quality evidence that pharmaceutical THC (with or without CBD) slightly improved anxiety in people with other medical conditions such as chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, and little evidence that cannabinoids treat anxiety disorders themselves. The authors concluded that there is not enough evidence to guide the use of cannabinoids for mental disorders.

One of the most cited studies in the field is a 2011 Brazilian trial in which 24 people with social anxiety disorder took a single 600 mg dose of CBD or a placebo (12 per group) before a simulated public speaking test. Compared to the placebo group, CBD-treated patients showed significantly reduced anxiety, cognitive impairment, and discomfort during their speech. The trial was small and tested a single dose, not ongoing use.

Research from Washington State University, published in 2018 in the Journal of Affective Disorders, analyzed nearly 12,000 real-world cannabis sessions logged in an app. Users perceived about a 58% reduction in anxiety and stress after smoking or vaping cannabis. However, baseline depression appeared to worsen over time with continued use, and because the users were self-selected and expectation effects couldn't be controlled, the results describe perceived short-term relief rather than proven treatment. This underscores the importance of moderation and intentional use rather than daily self-medication.

It is worth noting that most clinical trials have been relatively small and short-term. Large-scale, long-duration randomized controlled trials are still needed, and researchers caution against treating cannabis as a replacement for evidence-based anxiety treatments like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or prescribed medications without consulting a healthcare provider.

Strains and terpenes for anxiety

Beyond cannabinoid ratios, the terpene profile of a cannabis product can significantly influence its effects on anxiety. Terpenes are the aromatic compounds responsible for the distinct smell and flavor of different cannabis strains, and emerging research suggests they play an active role in modulating mood and stress responses.

Linalool, the terpene found abundantly in lavender, has demonstrated anxiolytic properties in animal studies. Strains high in linalool tend to promote calm without heavy sedation. Limonene, found in citrus peels, has been associated with elevated mood and stress relief. Myrcene, the most common terpene in cannabis, promotes relaxation and sedation at high levels — useful for nighttime anxiety but potentially too sedating for daytime use.

Beta-caryophyllene is particularly interesting because it is one of the few terpenes known to directly activate CB2 receptors in the endocannabinoid system. Animal research suggests it may have anti-anxiety and anti-inflammatory properties. It is found in black pepper, cloves, and many cannabis strains, which is the usual explanation given for chewing black peppercorns as a folk remedy for cannabis-induced paranoia, a remedy that has not been tested in clinical trials.

When selecting products for anxiety, look for strains or edibles with high CBD-to-THC ratios and terpene profiles rich in linalool, limonene, or beta-caryophyllene. Avoid high-THC strains with dominant myrcene profiles if you are using during the day, as the combination can be overly sedating.

Practical harm reduction tips

Talk to a clinician first. There is no established cannabis or CBD dose for treating anxiety. If you take any medication, ask your doctor or pharmacist before trying CBD or THC, because the FDA warns that CBD can raise or lower the effects of other drugs and adds to the drowsiness caused by alcohol, sleep aids, and anti-anxiety medications.

Start low and go slow with THC. If you choose to try THC, start at about 2.5 mg (1–2.5 mg if you are anxiety-prone or new to cannabis, and no more than 5 mg) and wait at least two hours before considering a second dose, especially with edibles. The delayed onset of edibles is the number one reason people overconsume and end up anxious.

Don't count on CBD as a safety net. CBD is often marketed as an antidote to THC anxiety, but a 2023 randomized trial found that adding 10–30 mg of CBD to 10 mg of THC did not reduce THC's acute adverse effects on cognition or mental health. The most reliable protection is a lower THC dose.

Control your environment. Set and setting matter with cannabis just as they do with other psychoactive substances. Consume in a safe, familiar, and comfortable environment. Avoid using cannabis in social situations that already make you anxious until you know how a specific product affects you.

Avoid daily use for anxiety management. While occasional cannabis use can provide short-term relief, frequent use raises the risk of cannabis use disorder (the CDC estimates about 3 in 10 people who use cannabis have it). Use cannabis as one tool among many — alongside therapy, exercise, meditation, and other evidence-based strategies — rather than as your sole coping mechanism.

Know when to seek help. If your anxiety is severe, persistent, or worsening, consult a mental health professional. Cannabis can complement a treatment plan, but it should not replace professional care, particularly for diagnosed anxiety disorders or co-occurring conditions.
